Exponentiation (g(g(n)))^r is the standard real power of a positive real base (base ≥1)

Comparison is between integers (left-hand side) and real numbers (right-hand side); conventional ordering on R is used
root_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Define S = { r ∈ R : ∃ g : N → N such that ∀ n ∈ N, g(n+1) - g(n) ≥ (g(g(n)))^r }. The problem asks for r_max = sup S and whether this supremum is attained (i.e. ∃ g for r = r_max). Equivalently: find the largest real r for which there exists at least one function g: N→N satisfying the stated universal inequality.
quantifier_order: Choose r ∈ R (we seek the largest such r)
There exists a function g : N → N (choice of g may depend on r)
For all n ∈ N, the inequality g(n+1) - g(n) ≥ (g(g(n)))^r holds

payload.theorem_nl:
Let $\mathbb{N} = \{1,2,3,\dots\}$. Find the largest real constant $r$ such that there exists a function $g\colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that
\[
g(n+1)-g(n) \geq (g(g(n)))^r
\]
for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: To prove the theorem, first exhibit a witness at the candidate value r=1/4. Lemma L3 shows that the explicit function g(n)=n^2 works for every r\le 1/4, hence in particular for r=1/4. Next prove sharpness: assume r>1/4 and suppose a witness g exists. Since r>0, Lemma L4 implies that g must be strictly increasing. Lemma L5 then rules out the existence of any such strictly increasing witness when r>1/4. Therefore no exponent larger than 1/4 is possible, while 1/4 itself is possible. Hence the largest real constant is 1/4, attained by g(n)=n^2.

steps.derives: There exists a function g : \mathbb N \to \mathbb N satisfying g(n+1)-g(n) \ge (g(g(n)))^{1/4} for all n\in\mathbb N.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply Lemma L3 with r = 1/4. The lemma gives an explicit witness, namely g(n)=n^2, and proves the required inequality for every n.

steps.derives: For any real r>1/4, every function g : \mathbb N \to \mathbb N satisfying g(n+1)-g(n) \ge (g(g(n)))^r for all n is strictly increasing and satisfies g(n)\ge n for all n.
steps.trivial_justification: Fix an arbitrary real r>1/4 and an arbitrary function g satisfying the inequality. Since r>1/4, in particular r>0, Lemma L4 applies directly and yields strict monotonicity and the estimate g(n)\ge n.

steps.derives: For any real r>1/4, there does not exist any function g : \mathbb N \to \mathbb N satisfying g(n+1)-g(n) \ge (g(g(n)))^r for all n\in\mathbb N.
steps.trivial_justification: Fix r>1/4. If such a function g existed, Step A2 would imply that g is strictly increasing. Lemma L5 says that no strictly increasing function can satisfy the inequality for such an r. This contradiction shows nonexistence of any witness g for every r>1/4.

steps.derives: The real number 1/4 is feasible, and every real number larger than 1/4 is infeasible.
steps.trivial_justification: Step A1 gives feasibility at r=1/4. Step A3 gives infeasibility for every r>1/4.

steps.derives: The largest real constant r such that there exists a function g\colon \mathbb N \to \mathbb N with g(n+1)-g(n) \ge (g(g(n)))^r for all n\in\mathbb N is r=1/4, and this largest value is attained by the explicit function g(n)=n^2.
steps.trivial_justification: A feasible value exists at r=1/4, while no larger real value is feasible. By the definition of largest feasible real constant, the answer is exactly r=1/4. Because Step A1 provides an explicit witness at r=1/4, the supremum is attained.

lemmas.statement_nl: Define \(g : \mathbb N \to \mathbb N\) by \(g(n)=n^2\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\). Then for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), one has \(g(n+1)-g(n)=2n+1\) and \(g(g(n))=n^4\).

lemmas.self_check_notes: For n=1 equality holds for all exponents; for n>1, monotonicity in the exponent gives the claim.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let \(r\in\mathbb R\) satisfy \(r\le \tfrac14\). Then for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), one has \(n^{4r}\le n\).

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Establishes feasibility for every r up to 1/4, in particular for r=1/4.
lemmas.self_check_notes: Combines the explicit formulas from the quadratic choice with the exponent bound n^{4r}\le n.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For r\le 1/4 and g(n)=n^2, one has g(n+1)-g(n)=2n+1 and (g(g(n)))^r=(n^4)^r=n^{4r}\le n\le 2n+1, so g(n+1)-g(n)\ge (g(g(n)))^r for all n.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let \(r\in\mathbb R\) satisfy \(r\le \tfrac14\). Define \(g : \mathbb N \to \mathbb N\) by \(g(n)=n^2\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\). Then for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), the inequality \(g(n+1)-g(n) \ge (g(g(n)))^r\) holds.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Reduces the upper-bound direction to the strictly increasing case and extracts the basic estimate g(n)\ge n.
lemmas.self_check_notes: Because g(g(n)) is a positive integer, its positive real power is at least 1.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: If r>0 and g(n+1)-g(n)\ge (g(g(n)))^r for all n, then g(n+1)-g(n)\ge 1 for all n, hence g(n+1)>g(n). By induction from g(1)\ge 1 and increments at least 1, g(n)\ge n for all n.
quantifier_order: Choose r in \mathbb R with r>0
Choose g : \mathbb N -> \mathbb N satisfying the inequality for all n

lemmas.statement_nl: Let \(r\in\mathbb R\) with \(r>0\), and let \(g : \mathbb N \to \mathbb N\) satisfy \(g(n+1)-g(n) \ge (g(g(n)))^r\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\). Then \(g(n+1)>g(n)\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), so \(g\) is strictly increasing, and consequently \(g(n)\ge n\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\).

lemmas.role_in_assembly: This is the decisive impossibility statement giving the sharp upper bound r\le 1/4.
lemmas.self_check_notes: This is the main hard lemma of the decomposition; it encapsulates the nonexistence argument for exponents above 1/4.

candidates.strategy_summary: Use an explicit quadratic witness to prove attainability at r = 1/4, and isolate the hard impossibility direction into a single self-contained upper-bound lemma showing that no strictly increasing integer-valued witness can exist for any r > 1/4.
